newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund futures sharply lower after slew of data.
newsitem.headline: Bund futures sharply lower after slew of data.

text.p: Bund futures were sharply lower on Wednesday as a slew of economic reports appeared on balance to not be as negative as traders had expected.
The June DTB Bund futures contract was down 45 basis points late in the day at 102.11 and had traded as low as 101.85.

Traders said flat fourth quarter German GDP growth and reports that Thursday's unemployment report will show an adjusted rise of no more than 20,000 were both stronger than had been expected -- hurting demand for Bunds.
German finance minister Theo Waigel, meanwhile, said the country can qualify for EMU if unemployment falls by summer.

Analysts said that if the jobs report does confirm that the economy is not as weak as had been expected, Bunds still have room to fall -- especially considering the number of long positions that had been taken recently.
Traders said that more EMU-optimistic remarks from Waigel could also add to Bunds' difficulties.
The Bund futures contract had climbed toward record highs recently, largley on unwinding of convergence trades from high-yielding bond markets.
Traders have little interest in Thursday's Bundesbank council meeting with rates seen on hold for some time.
Analysts said the combination of a greater chance that EMU will happen on schedule and the economic news triggered a fresh evaluation of the market's recent gains.
"A lot of people had been pessimistic about the economy," said Catherine Lee, bond market analyst at R.H. Wrightson & Associates. "There was a bit of a reassessment."
Expectations about stronger growth were revealed in a six basis point steepening of the yield curve to 214 basis points, reversing a flattening trend of recent sessions.
Analysts said much now hinges on Thursday morning's German unemployment report.

Economists said today's report that industrial output fell in January by 1.7 percent from the month before showed that the economy appeared on track once the impact of a decline in the construction sector was stripped away.
"The data signals a slight economic recovery overall and does not give the Bundesbank a reason to lower interest rates," said Lothar Hessler, economist at Trinkaus & Burkhardt.
